En entrant au Centre Toussaint, il est f: Walking into the Centre Toussaint, it’s easy to picture the bright, freshly renovated space buzzing with activity. You feel at ease right away, and the room is ready to welcome those, young and old, who are here to learn, chat and build connections. “It’s a place that brings everyone closer to Afro identity and Haitian culture, through classes and workshops,” explains founder Sly Toussaint, who has made it her mission for the past three years. With something for every taste and a varied program that includes classes in Creole, cooking, history, dance and more, the cultural centre answers a need felt across the community, and beyond.
« C’est une grande question : c’est le p: “That’s a big question: it’s the journey of a lifetime,” Sly says with a laugh when asked how she came to launch such a project. The idea behind the Centre Toussaint is closely tied to the path of the woman who was born in Montréal. “When I was nine, I went to live in Haiti. The economic and political situation had stabilized, so my mother wanted to go back.” Since she was young, her parents had gone back and forth between Port-au-Prince and Montréal. Her mother, who had fallen in love with Quebec, lives there full time. “My father couldn’t adapt to the climate and the Quebec system,” she says. She spent her formative years in Haiti, until she was 16. “Those were beautiful years,” she says. “When I came back to Montréal, I saw the scope, the sheer magnitude of the beauty of Haitian culture. A lot of people asked me questions about Haiti, the language, the culture, asked me what it was like.”
Dix ans plus tard, le temps de finir ses: Ten years later, after finishing her studies and taking on other projects, she chose to share her experience by founding a cultural centre. For Sly, coming back was far from easy. “It was very hard,” she says, describing the culture shock and the depression that followed. “I was in therapy for years.” She missed everything, especially the warmth, both the warmth of the weather and the affection of a people, a community. “I felt like life was going on without me. I had friends over there, who had friends, a future. I no longer had a vision of myself in the long term,” she confides. Today, Sly is thriving. Time has done its work, helping put things in perspective, as have the people who have crossed her path since. “You find the people you have things in common with, in terms of culture and values. They’re the ones who helped me find myself again and build the person I am today.”
<strong>« Que feriez-vous si vous saviez: “What would you do if you knew you couldn’t fail?”
« J’ai beaucoup de passions », dit Sly e: “I have a lot of passions,” Sly says, laughing. And it shows. “I love to sing, I love to dance, I love culture, languages.” After studying marketing and business administration, and after pursuing a parallel career in professional dance, she chose to build a place that reflects her and an entire community. Throughout her schooling, the young woman was aware of the obstacles others faced and also struggled in a system she didn’t know well. “I saw a lot of school dropouts, people who didn’t know what they wanted to do in life. Those things are very distressing, especially for people who are still developing,” she points out. “If you don’t take the right math classes, you won’t get into your CEGEP, into the career you want. It’s a lot of pressure for young people.” Ten years later, it was a Beyoncé and Jay-Z song, Nice, that inspired her. “What would you do if you know you couldn’t fail.
C’est une question que je me suis posée,: It’s a question I asked myself, to look beyond the obstacles.” The answer? A place to learn about Haitian culture in Montréal. She also acknowledges the contribution of all the members of the Haitian community who came before her and worked hard within their community, particularly on immigration and integration. “For those of us who were born here and grew up in this system, there’s nothing. There’s no place that lets us live our culture,” she explains.

<strong>‍</strong>Un tel endroit n’exist: ‍Such a place didn’t exist, so Sly created it. She speaks of the search for identity that marks those who move between two worlds. “Culture is a shared past, a shared history, a shared way of doing things. It’s something crucial in the quest for identity and for self-knowledge,” she believes. That’s why the famous social media memes about Haitian parents’ anecdotes, for example, bring together millennials from this culture.
Au Québec, ou ailleurs, ce ne sont pas t: In Quebec or elsewhere, not all children of Haitian immigrants learn the language, Creole. “When in Rome, do as the Romans do,” some believe. Others are simply too busy surviving. “Sometimes, the break is unconscious,” Sly says of the language and culture of origin. “People don’t take the time. They’re doing their best to raise their families and give them opportunities they never had. We forget to give what we were given,” she believes. She praises family members who teach their children the culture, or who make the effort to educate themselves.
« Ce n’est pas donné à tout le monde »,: “It’s not something everyone has access to,” the founder acknowledges. That’s where the cultural centre and the community come in. Along with classes and workshops, support groups are also offered to expectant parents. It’s a space for discussion to meet people who are facing the same issues. “We saw that it was a great need for people who are starting to have children. [For example], if I don’t speak Creole, how do I pass on to my child something I don’t have?” she says, describing the difficulties of those who navigate between two cultures. The Centre Toussaint is therefore not only for those of Haitian origin. Sly’s own family is multicultural.
Elle appelle chacun des membres à être l: She calls on every member of a family to be a keeper of each culture, making it a family effort rather than an individual one. She invites everyone who loves a Haitian person, or the culture, to explore it. “If you have a Haitian friend, why not learn more about their culture, their language, and connect with them on another level?” she asks. The Centre also aims to be as intergenerational as possible. “You’ll see people of all backgrounds in the groups: 30 to 40 per cent aren’t Haitian. And not all Black people are Haitian,” she says.
Sly Toussaint est également une passionn: Sly Toussaint is also passionate about history. The years she spent in her country of origin allowed her to learn more about her personal history and that of the country. “Knowing history helps you find yourself, find your place in the world,” she says. At the Centre Toussaint, history classes cover a range of subjects, from pre-colonial imperial Africa to the history of Black people in Quebec, a gap in history books and school curricula, according to the founder.
« On commence l’histoire des Noirs avec: “We start Black history with slavery, or to talk about the right to vote, and we don’t talk about what came before: before colonization, before America,” she laments. “One of the problems with Black history is that it’s taught as Black history and not also as white history, as the world’s history,” she continues. “In any dynamic, there are two sides. If Black people are fighting for their rights, who was standing in their way on the other side? It’s important to understand both sides of the coin, what was at stake on both sides. We all have a history that brought us here and led us to create what we create. It’s important to recognize that first and foremost, to take it into account.”
Au Centre Toussaint, tout se fait dans u: At the Centre Toussaint, everything is done from a Pan-African perspective. “We recognize that all Black people come from the same place: Africa,” explains the founder, who says that Haiti is Africa in the Americas, an observation that holds true, in her view, for any region with a population of African descent. “You crossed the ocean one way or another at some point in history, whether by force or by choice.”
Mené d’une main de maître par Sly Toussa: Led with a masterful hand by Sly Toussaint, the Centre that bears her name is first and foremost a community endeavour. “I’m very proud and fulfilled to have the team I have. Without these people, the Centre wouldn’t exist and wouldn’t be what it is,” she says. In the beginning, she taught Creole classes on her own, for free. An acquaintance approached her and said it was something she wanted to do as well. “It’s because she joined the team that I saw the project’s entrepreneurial potential. I told myself that if several people on the team taught other things, I could focus on the rest.” Now a seasoned entrepreneur, Sly encourages anyone who wants to start a project to go for it.
« On voit l'entrepreneuriat comme quelqu: “We see entrepreneurship as something distant, out of reach. Yet we’re all entrepreneurs,” she says. She gives the following example: “If you’ve ever moved, that’s a business.” You have to look for housing, choose it, stick to a budget, pick a neighbourhood and the number of bedrooms, coordinate the move, ask for help, set up a new space. “If you’ve ever asked for $5 for something, or done something in exchange for another service, you’re an entrepreneur. Demystifying that concept helps a lot,” she says.
« Beaucoup de nos mamans haïtiennes sont: “Many of our Haitian mothers are the first entrepreneurs we know,” she continues, citing cooking and hairdressing. And to get started, you take it one step at a time: you don’t have to quit your job, you begin and go slowly. That’s how things started for Sly and, three years later, the results speak for themselves. “I’d like every person of Haitian origin to set foot in the Centre,” she says in closing. We wish her that people keep rallying around and supporting the Centre Toussaint.
